title: Poetry Is Easier Than You Think — 2E

slides.prompt: Poem, not a poem, or not sure? Which one is BEST?
slides.stimulus: The rain is falling. The road is wet. People are going home.
slides.feedback: There is no one shape for a poem. Today we find out what poets actually do.
slides.hint: Do not worry about right or wrong. Tell me what you looked at to decide.
slides.notes: Beat 1 hook/diagnostic, 3 min. Sayable: Could this be a poem? Take 3 hands max: What makes you think so? Expect split vote, no-rhyme dominant. Log rhyme-as-rule misconception, do not correct yet. Bridge: Let's meet a real poet.

slides.prompt: What is this poem about? Which one is BEST?
slides.stimulus: "How do you like to go up in a swing, Up in the air so blue?" — Robert Louis Stevenson, The Swing
slides.feedback: The subject is ordinary — a child on a swing — but it feels exciting.
slides.hint: Look at the word that comes three times. What is it?
slides.notes: Beat 2 authentic model, 4 min. Read excerpt aloud twice. Expect near-unanimous B; D signals over-inference. Reveal, then elicit orally: Could you write about something ordinary — football, rain, your cat? Collect 4-5 ideas, no writing. Bridge: If a swing can be a poem, what about rhyme?

slides.prompt: Does a poem have to rhyme? Do comes and feet rhyme?
slides.stimulus: The fog comes on little cat feet. — from Carl Sandburg, Fog
slides.feedback: Some poems rhyme. Some do not. Rhyme is a tool, not a rule.
slides.hint: Say comes. Say feet. Same end sound?
slides.notes: Beat 3 misconception correction, 3 min. Have class say the pair aloud once if A appears. Log rhyme-as-rule. Bridge: If rhyme is not the secret, what makes these lines interesting? No cat picture — protects Beats 4-5 discovery.

slides.prompt: What picture do you see in your head?
slides.text: The fog comes on little cat feet. It sits looking over harbor and city on silent haunches and then moves on. — Carl Sandburg, Fog
slides.hint: Close your eyes. Fog moves — loud or quiet? Think: sits, looks, moves.
slides.notes: Beat 4 full-Fog camera, 4 min. Read aloud once at normal speed, once slowly. Accept any reasonable visual (cat, smoke, quiet animal sitting). Do NOT define personification yet. Reveal line (spoken): He does not explain fog. He makes us imagine it. Bridge: Fog cannot really sit. So what did the poet do?

slides.prompt: Can fog really have feet? Which one is BEST?
slides.stimulus: The fog comes on little cat feet.
slides.feedback: Fog has no feet. The poet gives fog a living action. This is ==personification==.
slides.hint: Does fog have legs? Where did the feet come from?
slides.notes: Beat 5 personification discovered, 4 min. 2E: elicit without verb bank first; frames available if stuck. After reveal show micro-examples orally: The wind whispers. The moon watches. The rain dances. Try-it orally: The door ___. The sun ___. Accept any living-action verb. Follow-up: Is the moon really watching? Bridge: Which words make pictures?

slides.prompt: Which one gives you a clearer picture? Which is BEST?
options: B. Cold rain taps on my window.
slides.answer: B. Cold rain taps on my window.
slides.feedback: B uses specific words — cold, taps, window — so you can see and hear it.
slides.hint: Which one can you see and hear? Which words help?
slides.notes: Beat 6 specific words, 4 min. Key line: Specific words make pictures. Counter long-word myth: Did B use difficult English? No — exact English. Try-it: The dog is nice. Change ONE word. Accept any specific verb. Bridge: Now watch one plain sentence become a poem.

slides.prompt: How can we make this more interesting?
items: The loud school bell shouts through the tired afternoon.
slides.notes: Beat 7 model sentence-to-poem, 4 min. Build orally BEFORE revealing each line. Sayables: What can we add? What stronger verb? Where does it shout? Accept variants (cries, hot evening). Say: We did not need difficult English. Final two-line break pre-teaches line breaks. Bridge: Those moves have names. Here are all five together.

slides.prompt: Your poet's toolbox — which choices can you use?
slides.text: 1. Specific words — cold rain taps. 2. Simile — moon like a lamp. 3. Personification — wind whispers. 4. Repetition — I wait, I wait. 5. Line breaks — rain / falls / tonight.
slides.notes: Beat 8 REQUIRED all-concepts synthesis, 4 min. All five visible from initial; nothing hidden, no new teaching. Say: These are your five choices. You only need one in your poem. Pupils repeat each example chorally. Point back: 1 in rain, 2-4 just now, 5 in the bell. Result line (spoken): Poetry is making choices with ordinary words. Bridge: Now test yourself — which tool is this?

slides.prompt: The moon smiles at me. Which tool is BEST?
slides.feedback: The moon cannot smile. The poet gives it a human action.
slides.hint: Can the moon really smile? Who smiles?
slides.notes: Beat 9A rapid classification. Fingers 1/2/3 vote before reveal. 2E: ask why not the other two? A is not simile — no like/as. Contrast distractors.

slides.prompt: My brother runs like the wind. Which tool is BEST?
slides.feedback: The poet compares running to wind with like.
slides.hint: Find the word like. What two things are compared?
slides.notes: Beat 9B. Expect confusion with personification (wind is non-human). Counter: Who runs? The brother — a person. The tool here is the comparison word like.

slides.prompt: Run, run, run! Which tool is BEST?
slides.feedback: The word run is repeated on purpose for effect.
slides.hint: How many times do you see run?
slides.notes: Beat 9C. C is neither comparison nor non-human action — no like/as, no living action given. Pacing: 4 min total for all three 9A/B/C.

slides.prompt: Turn on your poetry camera. What do you notice on a rainy afternoon?
slides.stimulus: See? Hear? Feel? What small thing do others ignore?
slides.hint: See shoes, sky, windows. Hear rain, voices, bells. Feel cold, wet socks.
slides.notes: Beat 10 guided idea generation, 5 min. Say: Do not invent a new world. Tell me what is really here. Build word bank publicly from pupil words (take 6-8: wet shoes, grey sky, noisy rain, cold floor, umbrellas, dripping bags, sleepy students, water on window). Accept feelings as valid material. Keep bank visible into Beat 11. Bridge: Now use these words. Let's write one together.

slides.prompt: Let's write a poem together. What does the rain do?
items: The rain taps on the window

visual.alt: Rainbow joining two sides over a bridge

slides.notes: Beat 11 guided construction, 5 min. Staged sayables: What does the rain do? Where? What does it sound like? Can we give it a human action? Verb choices if stuck: taps, knocks, sings. Emphasise verbatim: This is not a perfect poem. It is a poem because we made choices. Title decided explicitly. Leave visible into Beat 12; remove before Beat 15 so pupils cannot copy.

slides.prompt: Choose ONE thing for your poem. Point to it now.
slides.stimulus: Rain, friend, phone, football, cat or dog, school, moon, a place, something missed, something loved.
slides.hint: Which one can you see right now — outside, in your bag, at home?
slides.notes: Beat 12 choice/anxiety reduction, 2 min. Get visible commitment in 60 seconds (finger on choice, whisper to neighbour). Open choice, no key. Spoken line: One clear subject makes a stronger poem. Bridge: Here is a recipe if you need steps.

slides.prompt: A simple recipe — training wheels. Lines 1 to 4.
slides.notes: Beat 13 recipe part 1 of 2 (same wording halves; split only to fit limits), 3 min total. Read aloud once. Link to toolbox: line 5 uses simile, line 6 personification, line 7 repetition. Spoken: Skip a line if you need to. Keep 6 to 8 lines. 2E preview: strong writers, line 8 changes the feeling.

slides.prompt: A simple recipe — training wheels. Lines 5 to 8.
slides.notes: Beat 13 recipe part 2 of 2. Same beat, identical wording halves. Training wheels, not rules. Bridge: Plan in 30 seconds, then write.

slides.prompt: Plan in 30 seconds. Fill this for YOUR subject.
slides.stimulus: My subject ___. 3 notices ___. Verb ___. Like ___. It ___.
slides.hint: Model — rain: cold, window, grey. Verb: tap. Like tiny fingers. It waits.
slides.notes: Beat 14 model planning, 2 min. Model rain in 60 sec, then pupils fill silently. Say: Copy the frames. Use your own words. Thirty seconds. Rescue: Stuck? Steal from our word bank — cold, window, grey — then change one word. Circulate for blanks: first check subject + one notice. Spoken close: Notes first, lines second. Now turn notes into lines.

slides.prompt: Write your first poem — about ONE thing.
slides.task: Write your first poem — ONE thing. 6 to 8 lines with a title. Specific details and one tool. No rhyme needed.
slides.frame: My ___ ... It is like ___ . It ___ . Strong writers: add a second picture or change the feeling in the last two lines.
slides.notes: Beat 15 independent transfer, 8 min hard stop (timer). Conditions: 6-8 lines, title, specific details, at least ONE of simile/personification/repetition/line-breaks, no rhyme needed. 2E extension (slide hint + spoken after 5 lines): Strong writers: add a second picture or change the feeling in the last two lines. Rescue ladder spoken: What can you see? What does it do? What does it sound like? What is it like? If it were a person, what would it do? Circulate priority: one subject, lines appearing, one detail, one tool. Non-starters: point to Beat 14 frames, dictate starter My ___. Remove Beat 11 model from view. Do NOT heavily correct grammar.

slides.prompt: Read your poem like a poet. Can you make ONE line better?
slides.stimulus: Title? 6 to 8 lines? Specific words? One tool? Picture? Line breaks chosen?
slides.hint: Point to your weakest line. Add one specific word or like-comparison.
slides.notes: Beat 16 self-check/revise, 3 min: 1 min check, 2 min rewrite one line. Say: Do not ask, Is it perfect? Ask, Which line can I make better? Affirm revisions adding specificity or a tool even if grammar imperfect. Spoken close: Poets revise choices; one stronger line is enough today. Bridge: So what IS poetry, after doing it?

slides.prompt: So... what is poetry? Which one is BEST?
options: C. Choosing words to create images
slides.answer: C. Choosing words to create images
slides.feedback: Poetry is not difficult English. Poetry is about making choices.
slides.hint: Did your poem need big words? Did it need rhyme?
slides.notes: Beat 17 consolidation, 2 min. Say: Think about your poem. Expect C; if A/B replay Beats 3+6 evidence (comes/feet did not rhyme; cold/taps were not hard). Follow-up oral: What is one choice you made? Take 3 answers. Bridge: One last challenge — prove it in two lines.

slides.prompt: Turn this into TWO poetic lines.
slides.task: The moon is bright. Write two lines. Use TWO different tools in your two lines.
slides.notes: Beat 18 exit evidence/fresh transfer, 2 min. 2E stretch built into task: TWO different tools (vs one in base spine). Frame hint if stuck: The moon ___ (watches, smiles, waits) or like a ___ (lamp, light, eye). Possibles: The moon / watches me. OR The bright moon hangs / like a lamp in the sky. Reward any real choice — human action, comparison, strong break. Per share ask: What choice did the writer make? Final line: You have written a poem. Collect exit lines + Beat 15 poems as evidence.
